Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Copperfield is evaluating Redwood Private for an airgapped-like deployment in their GovCloud region. Primary concerns: ensuring no direct outbound egress from the model hosts, chain-of-custody for audit logs, KMS integration with their HSM, RBAC/SSO mapping to Okta, and proving SOC 2 controls. They want a controlled maintenance path for updates and an ops playbook for emergency patching. Next steps: topology template, SOC2 artifact bundle, lab test kickoff.

Topics noticed: network isolation, egress proxies, bastion jump hosts, collector-forwarding, immutable audit manifests, HSM-wrap key policies, SSO provisioning, canary upgrade plan.

Action items (auto-detected, not authoritative): send topology template; share SOC2 docs; schedule lab test; provide draft runbook.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Avery Morales: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Avery from Redwood, AE on the account. Today Samir and Jin will walk through the private deploy security patterns and we'll dig into airgap-ish requirements and audit logging provenance, so, uh, feel free to stop us at any point.

[00:23] Elena Ruiz: Thanks. To kick off—this is Elena, I'm CISO at Copperfield. We're specifically looking at a deployment model where our inference fleet is logically isolated and no model node can talk to the internet. We still need to be able to pull updates through a controlled window. Hoping you can show how Redwood supports that.

[00:38] Samir Patel: Absolutely. The short version: Redwood Private supports a private control plane and on-prem agents within your VPC; model hosts can be restricted to egress-only through an approved proxy or not allowed to egress at all. For airgapped scenarios we provide an update bundle you can import via an approved bastion. But let's step through options.

[01:05] Mark Conway: I guess first question—when you say "bundle" how big are these? We run on-prem on DGX-ish racks; we need to know about binary provenance, checksums, and that updates don't open outbound channels during install.

[01:22] Jin Park: Good point. Bundles are signed artifacts, SHA-256 manifests, and each package includes a signed manifest describing kernel versions, runtime, and model weights metadata. The install step can be performed offline; the bootstrap tool verifies signatures against a public key we provide. There is no hidden side-channel used during deployment.

[01:44] Priya Natarajan: You mentioned manifests — do you keep a chain-of-custody or tamper-evident log for those? Our audit team wants to prove that the same artifact installed in test matched prod.

[02:01] Samir Patel: We support immutable manifests and can integrate with your SIEM by shipping the signed manifest and attestation events to your collector. For high-assurance use cases customers often push signed attestations to an internal artifact repository and mirror those into their WORM-enabled storage for retention.

[02:26] Tomás Vega: On the KMS side—our policy requires an HSM-backed master key in our on-prem HSM. Does Redwood's agent allow external KMS or bring-your-own-key?

[02:39] Jin Park: Yes, BYOK is supported. For Private we can route envelope encryption to your KMS. The model runtime uses ephemeral data keys that are wrapped by your HSM master key. Tokens for KMS calls can be short-lived and bound to node identity via mTLS. We talked about integrating with your PKI earlier—this is the same pattern.

[03:05] Mark Conway: Are there any calls to Redwood control plane during inference—like heartbeat or telemetry—that would travel out? We need to understand exactly what flows cross the VPC boundary.

[03:18] Samir Patel: By default the agent will report health and metrics to the control plane; but in private on-prem there's a local control plane option where telemetry is forwarded to your internal observability and you can disable outbound telem. We can also queue messages for periodic export through a customer-managed proxy under your control.

[03:40] Elena Ruiz: So for SOC 2 evidence, we need verifiable audit logs. How do you guarantee log integrity?

[03:50] Jin Park: There are several patterns: 1) Forward unmodified logs to your SIEM over mTLS with mutual auth; 2) Produce signed audit bundles (log segments signed with node identity keys) that you can push to immutable storage; 3) Hash log segments into a Merkle-style ledger if you want tamper-evidence cross-system.

[04:20] Priya Natarajan: Hmm, Merkle ledger—do you provide tooling for that or is it customer-built?

[04:28] Samir Patel: We provide a lightweight client that can emit hashes and signed checkpoints to an endpoint. Some customers push those checksums into their blockchain or append-only store; others just store them in S3 with Object Lock. We can also integrate with an internal attestation service if you have one.

[04:49] Mark Conway: About ingress—our policy only allows traffic to model hosts from a specific set of internal subnets and via a secured inference ingress. How are connections authenticated?

[05:00] Jin Park: Connections are mTLS between the client proxy and model endpoints; we also support per-route API keys and token exchange for short-lived request credentials. For strict networks you can front model hosts behind an L4/NGFW and accept traffic only from an internal envoy layer.

[05:20] Elena Ruiz: Ok, let's talk about emergency patches. In an airgapped setup how would you roll critical security updates without opening a long-lived outbound path?

[05:31] Samir Patel: Typical pattern is a signed offline bundle staged in your update repository. You schedule a maintenance window, and the operations team uses a bastion jump host to pull the bundle onto the isolated network. The install stub verifies signatures and applies updates. If you need to produce status back to Redwood, that's done via a signed attestation file that you may choose to send out-of-band.

[05:58] Tomás Vega: That works. For compliance we're asked to map RBAC roles into our existing groups in Okta. Can you map Redwood roles to SAML groups?

[06:07] Jin Park: Yes, SSO with SAML/OIDC is supported. We can map IdP groups to Redwood roles and sync group membership via SCIM if you want automated provisioning. For Private deployments there's a local connector that proxies SCIM to the control plane or keeps provisioning local.

[06:30] Priya Natarajan: A practical question—how do we rotate KMS keys and ensure previously stored logs remain decryptable for audits?

[06:38] Samir Patel: Use envelope encryption with a key rotation policy. Old objects are rewrapped or you keep the previous KMS versions (key versions) so you can unwrap older keys. We can help produce a rotation playbook that demonstrates decryptability over time — important for auditors.

[06:58] Mark Conway: Are there any third-party hosts in the chain? Like does the update bundle ever rely on cloud storage we don't control?

[07:07] Jin Park: For Private on-prem, no. Bundles are delivered to you (e.g., signed tarball). For dedicated/resident in a cloud region we may host artifacts in a controlled bucket but we support downloading via your proxy. For your case we'll do BYO artifact storage.

[07:27] Elena Ruiz: Can you talk a bit about firewalling strategy—what minimum rules we need on the nodes and what you recommend for perimeter devices?

[07:36] Samir Patel: Minimum: deny all outbound by default, allow only internal control-plane CIDRs and the collector endpoint if forwarding logs. For perimeter: enforce stateful inspection, implement strict egress allow-list if any egress is allowed (e.g., update proxy IP and port), and use IDS/IPS for lateral movement detection. Host firewall should block all inbound except from the internal L4 load balancer.

[08:05] Mark Conway: Good. On detection and forensics, how do you surface traced requests and token usage for a given model invocation? We need correlation IDs that propagate from calling app to runtime.

[08:18] Jin Park: We inject correlation IDs at the proxy layer and carry them through runtime logs and traces. The runtime emits a request lifecycle log with request-id, user-id (or anonymous token), model-variant, and latency buckets. Those logs can be forwarded raw to your SIEM and joined with application logs.

[08:41] Priya Natarajan: Is there PII in logs? We need to know what to mask before forwarding.

[08:48] Samir Patel: By default we redact prompt text in audit logs, but you can configure full redaction or select fields. For high-sensitivity customers we enable a tokenization proxy that masks PII before logs leave the inference plane.

[09:05] Elena Ruiz: Thanks. Switching gears—auditors will want to see proof of concept that demonstrates controls. What does a lab test look like?

[09:14] Jin Park: We typically do a 2-week lab: 1) deploy a small cluster in your network with a sample workload; 2) run a test suite for egress and ingress control, patch/update path, KMS wrap/unwrap cycles, RBAC provisioning and revocation; 3) exercise audit log export and retention. We'll provide a checklist and an artifacts pack for your auditors.

[09:41] Mark Conway: Timeframe—how long to get a lab ready?

[09:45] Samir Patel: Depends on your infra. If you provide a small VLAN and DNS entries, many customers spin up in 3–5 business days. For airgapped networks with manual approvals, plan for a week to schedule the maintenance window and approvals.

[09:58] Priya Natarajan: About data residency—we have a requirement that no logs or model outputs leave our continental boundary. How strict can you be?

[10:07] Jin Park: Extremely strict: Private lets you keep telemetry and logs local, and you can disable any outward control plane traffic. If you need to export anything for Redwood support, that would be via an explicit export bundle you sign off on.

[10:25] Elena Ruiz: Competitor question: some vendors claim "airgapped" but still use periodic outbound beacons. How does Redwood differ?

[10:33] Samir Patel: We do not require outbound beacons. For fully isolated deployments there is no periodic telemetry unless you opt into a proxy/push model. We respect customer policies — where customers want us to receive nothing, we provide tooling to operate without our control plane.

[10:50] Mark Conway: Ok, small detail—what about time sync? Our network forbids external NTP.

[10:56] Jin Park: Nodes can sync to an internal time source under your control. If you want cryptographic attestation we can include a time-stamp from your local TPM/HSM during signing operations.

[11:10] Priya Natarajan: A question from the compliance team—what SOC 2 sections are most relevant and can you share mapping to Redwood controls?

[11:18] Samir Patel: Relevant: CC6 (system operations), CC7 (change management), CC9 (logical and physical access), CC8 (system availability) and CC3 (confidentiality) depending on your use. We'll provide a control matrix mapping each SOC 2 point to specific technical controls in the Private plan.

[11:38] Tomás Vega: Do you have an ISO 27001 statement too?

[11:43] Jin Park: Yes, we maintain ISO 27001 posture for hosted services and have guidance for Private deployments that map our secure design to ISO clauses. We'll include artifacts and the scope notes.

[11:55] Elena Ruiz: Wonderful. A specific ask—our auditors want to see a sample audit bundle that includes signed manifests, node certs at time of install, and a log segment proving a deployment step. Can you produce that?

[12:08] Samir Patel: We can produce a synthetic/sample bundle for the lab that contains all those pieces but scrubbed of customer data. For production, the attestation logs will come from your environment; we provide the format and can help validate the contents.

[12:25] Mark Conway: Final question—what's your recommended network topology for our use case?

[12:30] Jin Park: Our suggested topology: isolated VLAN for model hosts, NACLs + host firewall deny-all default, a maintenance bastion in a separate mgmt VLAN with strict jumpbox MFA, an internal artifact repository in the mgmt VLAN, a collector VM that pulls logs and forwards to your SIEM, and an optional egress proxy with allow-list for the limited maintenance window. We'll send a topology template.

[12:55] Elena Ruiz: Great, can you also include a short canary upgrade plan? We want to test upgrades on a 2-node slice before cluster-wide.

[13:03] Samir Patel: Yes — canary with traffic mirroring, test healthchecks, automatic rollback on certain failure signals. We'll include health thresholds and SLOs in the playbook.

[13:15] Priya Natarajan: Perfect. That's it from my side.

[13:19] Avery Morales: Thanks all. Quick recap of next steps and action items.

[13:23] Avery Morales: 1) We'll send the topology template and the SOC2/ISO artifact summary. 2) We'll produce a sample signed audit bundle and a lab checklist. 3) We'll propose dates for a 2-week lab. 4) Redwood SEs will collaborate with Copperfield infra to configure the KMS and the update bundle process.

[13:41] Elena Ruiz: Sounds good. We'll try to get approvals for a lab next week.

[13:45] Avery Morales: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up over email.

[13:50] (end)
